newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: Sharif pledges bold reforms for Pakistan economy.
newsitem.headline: Sharif pledges bold reforms for Pakistan economy.

text.p: Pakistan's prime minister-elect Nawaz Sharif said on Tuesday his government would implement "very bold reforms" to rescue an economy he said was ruined by the previous government of Benazir Bhutto. "Benazir Bhutto has totally destroyed our economy, so we'll have to bring in very bold reforms," he told a news conference in his home city of Lahore.
He was speaking after official results confirmed a landslide win for his Pakistan Muslim League in Monday's voting for a new National Assembly (lower house).
"Since we have an overwhelming majority, we are preparing a fresh agenda" for reforms, Sharif said, adding that he would be ready to talk about them in detail in three or four days.
The elections were forced by President Farooq Leghari's dismissal of Bhutto's government on November 5 on corruption and other charges, all of which she denies.
Bhutto, whose Pakistan People's Party (PPP) was humiliated in the elections, has complained bitterly of rigging even though international observers say they saw only minor irregularities.
She has hinted she may not accept the results, threatening more of the political instability that has bedevilled Pakistan, but Sharif said he believed Bhutto would concede in the end.
"This is what she says now, but later she will accept the results of the elections because everyone else will," he said.
With 177 results declared for the 217-seat National Assembly, the PML had won 124 seats against 15 for the PPP.
Sharif suggested he would abide by tough economic decisions made by the caretaker government Leghari installed, including conditions for a loan from the International Monetary Fund.
These include reducing the budget deficit to four percent of gross domestic product in the 1996/97 (July-June) financial year from 6.3 percent in 1995/96.
"I think we'll go along with all those points which are in the interests of the country, and I am sure that was the intention when the programme was being framed," he said.
"I also feel there will be room for reforms we are contemplating," Sharif added.
The wealthy industrialist said he envisaged rationalisation of the tax system, drastic spending cuts to help manage Pakistan's heavy debt burden and creating an investor-friendly environment.

"We will provide more and more incentives in the shape of tax holidays and tax reforms to the investor," he said in his sprawling home that swarmed with well-wishers and party faithful, who were beating drums, waving flags and dancing.
He also said he wanted to make the rupee fully convertible. "I think if we have any restrictions on the rupee, foreign exchange, they will have to be removed completely," he said.

Sharif was clearly delighted with election results that surpassed his expectations. "I was expecting a comfortable majority, but this is something more than a comfortable majority and I wasn't expecting that," he said.

His absolute majority will give him leverage in dealing with several controversial moves by Leghari after he dismissed Bhutto, including the establishment of a Council for Defence and National Security (CDNS), which gives military leaders a formal advisory role in government for the first time.
The military has ruled Pakistan for nearly half its 50-year existence and there has been loud criticism of the council, but Sharif was cautious when pressed on whether he would scrap it.
"The CDNS will have to be given a fresh look. This subject might come under discussion in the National Assembly. The parliament will decide whether the CDNS is required or not," he said.
